topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; framework may require adaptation for Australian health systems, different regulatory environments, and workforce structures.
takeaways: Use the identified competency framework to assess current capability gaps in your team's digital health literacy and prioritise upskilling in areas most relevant to your organisational context.

The framework provides a structured reference for designing AI literacy training programs specific to public health roles, helping target content to different professional levels rather than one-size-fits-all approaches.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on faculty development in public health education contexts; applicability to other sectors and non-academic settings unclear without access to full article.
takeaways: Faculty development programs are more effective at shifting AI literacy from resistance to readiness than top-down mandates — invest in peer learning and guided exploration for skeptical staff.

Public health educators face specific barriers to AI adoption (ethical concerns, data privacy, domain-specific applications); tailor literacy programs to address sector-relevant use cases rather than generic AI concepts.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - Sage Journals
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  Sage Journals
articles.generalisability: Generalisability is limited by the lack of detail in the snippet; the focus on Generation Z may not apply equally to older worker populations or different cultural contexts. Educational strategies' effectiveness would depend on implementation context and institutional resources.
takeaways: Identify gaps between current curricula and AI competencies your organisation requires, then partner with educational providers to co-design upskilling programs that combine technical skills with critical thinking about AI's implications.

For younger cohorts entering your workforce, establish mentorship or structured induction programs pairing Gen Z employees with experienced staff to translate formal AI literacy into practical workplace problem-solving.

Assess which 'innovative' educational modalities (e.g., project-based learning, simulation, cross-functional AI literacy modules) your organisation can pilot with early-career hires before rolling out broader training.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to middle school education context; applicability to adult workforce AI literacy development requires careful adaptation, as pedagogical approaches differ significantly between adolescent and adult learners.
takeaways: A holistic digital literacy framework should embed AI competencies alongside traditional digital skills rather than treating AI as a standalone topic—consider how to integrate AI literacy into existing skill development programs in your organisation.

Middle school frameworks may inform foundational AI literacy concepts (e.g., understanding algorithms, data basics, ethical reasoning) that could be adapted for adult employees with no prior AI exposure.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to higher education context; applicability to corporate employee development settings unclear without reviewing full methodology. Findings may not generalise to non-academic organisations or industries outside tertiary education.
takeaways: Consider structuring AI literacy programmes around a four-domain framework rather than treating it as a single skill — this meta-skill approach may help employees understand how AI competencies interconnect and apply across different workplace contexts.

In designing upskilling initiatives, map which of the four domains are most critical for your organisational roles (e.g. technical, strategic, ethical, or operational) to tailor training rather than delivering one-size-fits-all AI literacy.
Use the model to identify gaps in management capability — academic leaders may need different AI literacy emphasis than individual contributors, suggesting differentiated development pathways.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context, which may not directly transfer to corporate workplace settings. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Higher education strategies for AI literacy (e.g., curriculum design, interdisciplinary approaches) can inform corporate training programme structure, though adult learners and workplace constraints differ from university students.

Competency frameworks developed in academic settings provide a reference point for defining AI skill levels in organisations, but will need adaptation to align with job roles and business priorities rather than general education objectives.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: AI usage and employee creativity: the mediating role of work engagement and the moderating role of technology acceptance - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI usage and employee creativity: the mediating role of work engagement and the moderating role of technology acceptance  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The theoretical model (AI usage → work engagement → creativity, moderated by technology acceptance) is likely applicable across sectors, but findings may be limited by sample geography, industry focus, and organisational context.
takeaways: Work engagement acts as a key mechanism linking AI tool adoption to creative output — organisations should design AI implementations that enhance rather than undermine employee engagement through role clarity, autonomy, and meaningful work.
Employee technology acceptance is critical; investing in change management, training, and stakeholder involvement before and during AI rollout can amplify the creativity benefits of AI usage.

Monitor both engagement and acceptance metrics when introducing AI — low adoption of tools may signal disengagement or scepticism that, if unaddressed, will suppress the creative gains you expect from AI investment.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings may be context-dependent given focus on paternalistic leadership, which is more prevalent in certain cultures (particularly East Asian organisations); generalisability to Western organisations with different leadership styles requires caution.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by allowing them to customise and adapt systems to their workflows—this increases willingness to collaborate with AI rather than resist it.

Leaders should balance autonomy with supportive guidance when introducing AI; paternalistic leadership that combines clear direction with genuine concern for employee welfare may enhance AI adoption more effectively than purely directive or purely hands-off approaches.

Design AI implementation processes that let employees 'craft' their relationship with the technology—personalising interfaces, workflows, and use cases—rather than imposing one-size-fits-all deployment.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.article_type: Empirical study (likely cross-sectional or experimental design)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings depend on sample characteristics not disclosed in snippet. The psychological mechanisms (self-efficacy, transformational leadership) are likely generalisable across sectors and geographies, but the specific context and sample size are unknown.
takeaways: Develop transformational leadership capabilities in managers overseeing AI implementation — leaders who inspire and challenge employees to think differently can reduce job insecurity perceptions during organisational AI adoption.

Build employee self-efficacy proactively through targeted upskilling programmes and confidence-building activities before and during AI rollout, as this appears to buffer against job insecurity concerns.

Communicate clearly about AI's role (augmentation, not replacement) and invest in development opportunities — employees with higher self-efficacy and supportive leaders experience lower job insecurity despite technological change.

articles.title: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full article — depends on sample size, sector focus (cybersecurity), and geographic scope. Findings on job stress and AI self-efficacy as mediators of cybersecurity behaviour may be specific to security-focused roles and may not transfer directly to broader employee populations in Australia.
takeaways: Build AI self-efficacy in security-critical roles as a psychological buffer — employees with stronger confidence in their ability to work with AI show more protective cybersecurity behaviours even under high job stress.

Monitor job stress levels in teams managing AI-related security tasks; high stress alone may undermine safe practices unless paired with targeted self-efficacy training and psychological safety measures.

Design AI capability development programmes that explicitly address anxiety and uncertainty in security contexts — framing AI as a tool employees can learn to use confidently may reduce defensive avoidance or risky shortcuts.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — full sample characteristics, geography, and sector scope cannot be determined without access to the complete article.
takeaways: Psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) may be a key lever for helping employees view AI tools as enablers rather than threats, potentially reducing resistance to algorithm-driven work.

Organisations seeking to drive innovation in AI-integrated roles should assess and build employees' psychological capital alongside AI tooling — this addresses the human-side barrier to effective adoption.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused perspective from the American Psychological Association; findings and recommendations may reflect US-specific labour market conditions, employment practices, and regulatory context that differ from Australian workplace norms.
takeaways: Acknowledge that workforce uncertainty around AI adoption is a psychological and organisational challenge requiring deliberate communication strategies — help leaders articulate clear timelines, upskilling pathways, and job security commitments to reduce anxiety and maintain engagement.

Design regular check-ins and psychological safety mechanisms to surface employee concerns about AI implementation early, rather than allowing uncertainty to compound and affect retention and performance.

Consider the mental health and wellbeing implications of rapid AI-driven change — proactive support through training, mentoring, and clear role clarity can mitigate stress and build confidence in new AI-enabled workflows.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a perspective piece from Stanford GSB without specified empirical sample, research methodology, or geographic scope. Likely reflects US higher education and business context.
takeaways: Identify specific AI-driven work changes relevant to your organisation (e.g., task automation, skill requirements, role redesign) rather than treating 'AI reshaping work' as a single phenomenon — different sectors and roles will experience different shifts.

Proactively map which employee behaviours, mindsets, and capabilities need to shift in response to AI adoption in your context, then design targeted behaviour change interventions rather than assuming generic upskilling alone will address transition challenges.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not fully detailed in snippet — geographic scope, sector coverage, and sample size are unclear from title alone.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption communications around opportunity and skill development (approach motivation) rather than threat and job loss (avoidance motivation) to encourage proactive job crafting and adaptation.

Monitor whether employees are engaging in constructive job crafting (seeking new responsibilities) versus defensive job crafting (withdrawing or minimising AI-related tasks) during implementation, as this affects engagement and performance outcomes.
Provide employees with agency in how they incorporate AI into their roles — those who feel they can shape their work design are more likely to adapt constructively rather than resist or disengage.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on global client experience and surveys, but specific sample composition and geographic weighting are unclear. Findings may reflect patterns most visible in large organisations and developed economies.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce development challenge, not just a technology implementation, to secure buy-in from HR and people leaders who shape change management strategy.
Identify which roles and skill groups will need reskilling versus upskilling, then design targeted capability-building programmes before AI rollout to reduce resistance and redundancy anxiety.

Treat workforce transformation as concurrent with AI deployment, not a follow-up—embedding learning and role redesign into the implementation timeline increases adoption velocity and employee engagement.

articles.title: Advancing applied behavioral science: the GAP framework - Nature
articles.snippet: Advancing applied behavioral science: the GAP framework  Nature
articles.generalisability: Framework-level applicability is potentially broad, though generalisability depends on empirical validation across contexts not evident from the snippet alone.
takeaways: The GAP framework (likely Goal-Action-Prompt or similar) provides a structured approach to designing behaviour change interventions—use it to map the specific goal, identify the action barrier, and design the prompt or nudge needed for your AI capability development program.

Applying a formal behavioural science framework to organisational change increases the likelihood of sustained adoption compared to ad-hoc approaches; consider documenting your intervention logic using this or similar frameworks when rolling out AI literacy initiatives.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across sectors, but specific client examples and implementation contexts not detailed in snippet; may reflect larger organisations' capabilities more than SMEs.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling as an organisational change initiative requiring leadership commitment and structural support, not just individual training programs—this shifts accountability from learners to the system.
Integrate AI capability development into broader business transformation roadmaps rather than treating it as a standalone HR or IT function to increase relevance and adoption.
Design upskilling interventions around job-specific workflows and pain points employees actually experience, making learning directly applicable to their daily work and reducing resistance to change.

articles.title: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — full methodology not provided. Generalisability depends on study design, sample characteristics, and whether findings are based on empirical data or theoretical framework. Recommend reviewing full article for details on geographic scope, sample size, and sector coverage.
takeaways: Design AI systems with inclusive principles from the outset, then layer DEI interventions on top — culture and policy work together to moderate how employees experience algorithmic decision-making.

Assess your current diversity-supportive culture before rolling out AI tools; weak culture amplifies the risk that algorithmic systems will be perceived as unfair or exclusionary, even if technically neutral.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample size and composition, which are not detailed in the snippet provided. The findings relate to fundamental cognitive-personality mechanisms likely applicable across populations, but specific limitations cannot be assessed without full methodology.
takeaways: People with different personality traits remember surprising moments in strikingly different ways — some personalities appear to 'stick' unexpected events in memory better than others, which is counterintuitive since we often assume everyone finds surprising events equally memorable.

Your personality may act as a filter for what your brain decides to encode and keep: introverts, extroverts, or those high in neuroticism might naturally remember a shocking meeting or unexpected feedback quite differently, even if they witnessed the same event.

This hints at why eyewitness accounts of surprising events vary so wildly between people — it's not just about attention or interest, but also something deeper about how your personality wires your memory system.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — the geographic scope, sample size, and methodology are not detailed, so generalisability cannot be assessed.
takeaways: Language choices in everyday activities like wine reviewing can reveal personality traits — a fun reminder that what we write casually says more about us than we might think.
AI can detect personality patterns in written text where humans might see only superficial differences, opening up quirky new ways to understand what makes people tick.
Wine reviews are unexpectedly rich data for personality analysis, suggesting that hobbies and consumer preferences are windows into deeper psychological traits.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — typical neuroscience news reports cite single studies with small sample sizes; actual research scope unclear from snippet alone.
takeaways: The headline promises a 'shocking difference' in psychopathic brains, but the actual finding is likely more nuanced than popularised — brain imaging differences exist but don't determine behaviour or personality.

Psychopathy exists on a spectrum and includes traits like fearlessness and reduced empathy that aren't inherently criminal; brain differences alone can't explain why some individuals with these traits harm others while others don't.

Brain scan headlines often oversell findings — fascinating neurological differences make for clickable stories, but correlation between brain structure and complex human traits like psychopathy remains messy and contested among researchers.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on twin study methodology and sample characteristics not detailed in snippet; twin studies typically have limitations in representing broader populations and may not capture environmental or cultural factors fully.
takeaways: Twin studies suggest authoritarian political beliefs have a heritable genetic component, challenging the assumption that such views are purely learned or ideological — which is counterintuitive to many people's intuitions about politics and persuasion.

The finding that genetics plays a role doesn't mean beliefs are fixed or unchangeable; it highlights how nature and nurture interact in shaping political worldviews, making it a more nuanced story than either 'nature' or 'nurture' alone.

This research is a good reminder that deeply held political convictions — which feel reasoned and chosen — may have biological roots we're largely unaware of, which is a fascinating window into why political persuasion is so difficult.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — appears to be a multi-country investigation examining universal patterns in music preference across diverse populations.
takeaways: People with similar personality traits gravitate toward the same music genres worldwide, suggesting personality and taste are linked by something deeper than culture alone.

Your music playlist might be a surprisingly accurate window into your personality — a fun way to think about why that friend with a completely different taste in music also seems to have a completely different outlook on life.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear without access to full article — findings may be from a single study with unknown geographic scope and sample characteristics.
takeaways: There's an unexpected biological connection between thyroid hormones and personality expression — hyperthyroidism correlates with darker personality traits like narcissism, Machiavellianism, or psychopathy.
This challenges the common assumption that personality is purely psychological; it hints that physiological conditions can influence how people present themselves socially and interpersonally.

The finding is counterintuitive because we typically think of thyroid disorders in terms of metabolism and energy, not personality — making it a fun example of how the body's chemistry might shape character traits in surprising ways.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified from snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings specific to academic settings with multicultural teams; generalisability to corporate or other organisational contexts unclear from available information.
takeaways: AI tools can be designed to support inclusive leadership practices that improve outcomes for underrepresented groups (including women); consider how algorithmic assistance might help leaders recognise and counteract unconscious bias in team dynamics and decision-making.

In multicultural academic environments, AI-assisted approaches may help surface equity issues around gender that might otherwise be overlooked; audit your own team processes for similar blind spots and test whether structured, data-informed practices improve psychological safety for all members.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Moderate to good — PwC's global workforce surveys typically reach large, multinational samples across sectors, though sample composition and response rates are not detailed in the snippet. Findings may skew toward larger organisations and developed economies.
takeaways: Identify which specific workforce anxieties (job security, AI displacement, work conditions) are most prevalent in your organisation by comparing internal sentiment data against this global benchmark.

Use hopes vs. fears data to tailor psychological safety communications — address concrete fears (e.g. AI job replacement) with transparent upskilling or role transition support, rather than generic reassurance.
Segment results by role, geography, and tenure to pinpoint which employee cohorts need most support, since global averages may mask acute safety concerns in specific teams or demographics.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology — depends on sample size, sector, and geographic scope. The relationship between AI adoption, psychological safety, and depression warrants testing across different organisational contexts and geographies before drawing broad conclusions.
takeaways: AI adoption can harm mental health if it erodes psychological safety — leaders must actively foster a climate where employees feel safe raising concerns about AI systems, asking questions, and admitting uncertainty without fear of penalty.

Ethical leadership is a protective factor during AI transitions — explicitly modelling transparent decision-making about AI use, acknowledging risks openly, and involving employees in AI governance can mitigate depression and anxiety among staff.

Screen for psychological safety early in AI implementation: assess whether employees feel valued and safe speaking up about AI-related worries before rolling out systems, and adjust adoption strategy if safety is compromised.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's perspective is informed by consulting work with large organisations, likely skewing toward multinational firms and developed economies. The specific organisational contexts and sample sizes are not detailed, limiting applicability to smaller or different sector organisations.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that invite diverse viewpoints and lower the interpersonal risk of speaking up — this helps level advantages held by senior or majority-group employees and improves decision quality.

Measure psychological safety alongside other team metrics to track progress; BCG likely provides diagnostic tools or frameworks you can adapt to assess where psychological safety gaps exist in your own teams.

articles.title: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — likely reflects patterns in knowledge-work sectors, primarily US-based HBR readership, but specific organisational contexts and regulatory environments (e.g., Australia's privacy frameworks) may differ.
takeaways: Identify and address the specific fears or concerns driving non-transparency about AI use — whether fear of job loss, performance scrutiny, or policy violation — as these vary by role and organisational culture.

Create explicit, psychologically safe channels for employees to report AI usage without penalty; transparency policies alone fail if employees don't trust they won't be blamed for experimentation or mistakes.

Establish clear, written guidelines on acceptable AI use that distinguish between approved tools and prohibited ones, reducing ambiguity that often leads employees to stay silent rather than risk misinterpretation.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — SHRM guidance reflects US HR practices and cultural context; core leadership principles are broadly applicable, but specific recommendations may need localisation for Australian workplace norms and employment law.
takeaways: Identify the specific leadership behaviours (e.g. soliciting input, responding non-defensively to challenges, admitting mistakes) that create psychological safety in your team, and model them consistently to shift team norms.

Use team meetings or one-on-ones to explicitly invite dissent and low-stakes experimentation, then respond to mistakes or contrary opinions with curiosity rather than blame to reinforce that speaking up is safe.
Audit your own reactions to bad news or failure: leaders' first response often sets the tone for psychological safety more powerfully than any policy document.
